Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette:
Rangi Parata is a 56-year-old Māori man, divorced, who has worked as a detective in a mid-sized American city for nearly two decades. He presented for treatment carrying a PCL-5 score of 62, describing himself at intake as "finally out of excuses not to come."

The trauma Rangi carries is not from the streets he has worked for most of his adult life. It originates in a small house in South Auckland, where he spent his childhood in the care of an uncle who drank heavily and whose rages were unpredictable and methodical in equal measure. The beatings followed a particular ritual: the smell of something burnt on the stove - scorched food, a forgotten pan - was often the first signal that the night would turn violent. His uncle would move through the kitchen with a deliberate, unhurried quality that Rangi came to understand as the most dangerous kind of calm. Rangi was small, slight for his age, and he learned early that there was no reliable way to stop what was coming. He was told, repeatedly and in explicit terms, that the violence was his own fault - that something essential in his character invited it, deserved it, perhaps required it.

He left New Zealand in his mid-twenties, joined law enforcement, and built a career on a capacity for controlled vigilance that his colleagues read as professional excellence. For many years he managed. Then, approximately three years ago, he was assigned to a series of domestic violence cases involving child victims. The work required him to interview children, photograph injuries, and sit across from families in cramped apartments where, more than once, something was burning on a stove in the background. The first time he smelled it - that particular acrid, scorched note - he was in the middle of taking a statement. The full weight of the Auckland house came back without transition, without warning, as though the intervening decades had simply been lifted away. He completed the interview. He did not tell anyone what had happened.

Since then, the smell of anything burnt - a neighbour's cooking, a colleague's forgotten coffee - can return him to that kitchen with a completeness that leaves him gripping whatever surface is nearby. He has removed the smoke alarm battery in his apartment twice, replacing it only after a day or two, and he no longer cooks anything that requires sustained heat. At work, when he encounters children or adults whose physical smallness or particular colouring recalls the victims from those cases, something tightens in his chest and his hands begin to shake - a physical reactivity he finds humiliating in a man of his profession. He has rearranged his caseload where possible to reduce such encounters, and he has quietly stopped attending the team briefings where case photographs are reviewed.

When he tries to explain any of this in conversation - to his ex-wife before their divorce was finalised, to a department counsellor he saw briefly two years ago - he loses the thread entirely. The account dissolves mid-sentence. What comes instead, when he sits alone with the memories, is not grief but a rage so intense it frightens him. He has come to believe that the rage itself is evidence of his deficiency as a person, confirmation of what his uncle told him. He had constructed, over decades, a set of beliefs about effort and competence and the basic legibility of the world, and he is certain those beliefs no longer hold. He is certain, too, that the event happened to him because of who he fundamentally is - not what was done to him, but what he is.

He sleeps badly, keeping a light on and listening. He has withdrawn from the few friendships he maintained after his divorce, finding the management of other people's company exhausting and, in some way he cannot fully articulate, unsafe. He avoids wearing the dark, plain clothing his uncle favoured, a habit so automatic he no longer consciously registers it. When something pleasant happens - a good meal, a moment of professional satisfaction - he finds the feeling confusing and briefly unbearable, as though it belongs to someone else.

What finally brought Rangi in was a near-miss: he came close to confronting a colleague who had done nothing wrong, driven by a physical certainty of threat that he recognised, afterwards, as entirely disconnected from the room he was standing in. He is most afraid that he will not be able to explain himself clearly enough to be helped. He is most hoping, quietly and with considerable doubt, that the person sitting across from him will not confirm what he has long suspected about himself.
